title: Information Disclosure via Unauthenticated /configs Endpoint
description: The /configs endpoint at api.axross-recipe.com returns sensitive internal configuration data without any authentication. This includes organization IDs, JupyterHub access lists, recipe creation permissions, comment-restricted organizations, terms update timestamps, and internal database coexistence comments.
impact: An attacker can enumerate internal organization IDs, identify which organizations have JupyterHub access, which can create recipes, and which have restricted commenting. This information can be used to target specific organizations, understand the internal structure of the platform, and plan further attacks. The leaked organization IDs (37, 53, 180, 557, 629, 639 for JupyterHub; 37, 53, 131, 56, 142, 211, 531, 944, 986, 1009, 1085 for recipe creation) provide a direct attack surface for targeted phishing or privilege escalation attempts.
technical_analysis: The /configs endpoint is a Rails API endpoint that returns all application configuration records without any authentication check. The endpoint returns an array of config objects, each containing: id, key, value, created_at, updated_at, transferable, virtual_id, virtual_params, config_type, value_json, and available_in_client. Sensitive data exposed includes: jupyterhub_orgs (organization IDs with Jupyter access), create_recipe_orgs (organization IDs that can create recipes), ng_comment_orgs (organization IDs with restricted commenting), coexist_db_comments (internal notes about database coexistence), and common_updated_terms_at (terms update timestamp). The endpoint is accessible via a simple GET request with no authentication headers required.
poc_description:
1. Send a GET request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/configs
2. Observe the response contains all application configuration data
3. No authentication headers or session cookies are required
remediation_steps:
1. Add authentication checks to the /configs endpoint to ensure only authenticated users with appropriate permissions can access it
2. Review which config fields need to be exposed to the client (available_in_client flag) and restrict sensitive data
3. Implement proper authorization checks for all configuration endpoints
4. Consider using a separate, authenticated admin endpoint for sensitive configuration data

title: User Enumeration via Unauthenticated /users/{id} Endpoint
description: The /users/{id} endpoint at api.axross-recipe.com returns user profile data without any authentication. This allows an attacker to enumerate all users on the platform by iterating through user IDs, collecting names, avatar URLs, and role information.
impact: An attacker can enumerate all registered users on the platform, collecting usernames, profile information, and role assignments. This information can be used for targeted phishing attacks, social engineering, username enumeration for credential stuffing, and identifying high-privilege users. The ability to distinguish between existing and non-existing user IDs also enables user enumeration attacks.
technical_analysis: The /users/{id} endpoint is a Rails API endpoint that returns user profile data without any authentication check. The endpoint returns a JSON object containing: id, name, avatar URL, introduction, role, and transferred status. Existing users return HTTP 200 with user data, while non-existing users return HTTP 404 with {"result":"not found"}. This difference in response codes enables automated user enumeration. The endpoint is accessible via a simple GET request with no authentication headers required.
poc_description:
1. Send a GET request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/users/1
2. Observe the response contains user data (name, role, avatar URL)
3. Send a GET request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/users/999999
4. Observe the response returns {"result":"not found"}
5. The difference in responses allows automated user enumeration
poc_script_code:
#!/bin/bash
# Enumerate users by iterating through IDs
for id in 1 10 50 100 500 1000; do
  result=$(curl -s "https://api.axross-recipe.com/users/$id")
  name=$(echo "$result" | python3 -c "import sys,json; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(d.get('name','NOT_FOUND'))" 2>/dev/null)
  echo "User $id: $name"
done
remediation_steps:
1. Add authentication checks to the /users/{id} endpoint to require authentication
2. Return consistent responses for both existing and non-existing users to prevent enumeration
3. Consider implementing rate limiting on user ID lookups
4. Review whether public user profiles need to expose the role field

title: Information Disclosure via Unauthenticated /courses Endpoint
description: The /courses endpoint at api.axross-recipe.com returns all course data (approximately 98KB) without any authentication. This exposes course titles, descriptions, and potentially sensitive educational content to unauthenticated users.
impact: An attacker can enumerate all courses available on the platform, including their descriptions and metadata. While courses may be intended to be publicly visible, the lack of authentication on this bulk data endpoint could expose course structures, pricing information, and other metadata that could be used for competitive analysis or targeted attacks.
technical_analysis: The /courses endpoint is a Rails API endpoint that returns all course records without any authentication check. The endpoint returns a large JSON array (98KB) containing course objects with titles, descriptions, and other metadata. The endpoint is accessible via a simple GET request with no authentication headers required.
poc_description:
1. Send a GET request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/courses
2. Observe the response contains all course data (98KB)
3. No authentication headers or session cookies are required
poc_script_code: curl -s https://api.axross-recipe.com/courses | python3 -c "import sys,json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); print(f'Total courses: {len(data)}'); [print(f'  - {c[\"id\"]}: {c[\"title\"]}') for c in data[:10]]"
remediation_steps:
1. Add authentication checks to the /courses endpoint if the data should be protected
2. If courses are meant to be public, consider implementing pagination and rate limiting
3. Review what course metadata is exposed and whether any fields contain sensitive information

title: CSRF on Signup Endpoint - No Anti-CSRF Token Required
description: The signup endpoint at POST /signup on api.axross-recipe.com does not require any CSRF token, origin header check, or SameSite cookie validation. An attacker can craft a cross-origin HTML form that, when visited by a victim, silently submits a registration request to create a new user account.
impact: An attacker can force a victim's browser to create a user account on Axross Recipe without the victim's knowledge or consent. This can be used for account creation spam, phishing setups, or as a precursor to other attacks.
technical_analysis: The signup API endpoint at POST /signup on api.axross-recipe.com accepts JSON payloads with name, email, and password fields. The endpoint returns {"result":"success"} for valid registration data. No CSRF token, Origin header, or Referer header validation is performed. The NextAuth.js CSRF protection (__Host-next-auth.csrf-token cookie) is only used for NextAuth-specific endpoints, not for the application's own API endpoints on api.axross-recipe.com.
poc_description: 1. Send a POST request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/signup with JSON data containing name, email, and password fields. 2. No CSRF token or session cookie is required. 3. The endpoint returns {"result":"success"} indicating the account was created.
remediation_steps: 1. Implement CSRF protection on all state-changing API endpoints. 2. Validate the Origin and/or Referer headers on all state-changing requests. 3. Implement anti-CSRF tokens tied to the user session. 4. Use SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax cookies for session cookies.

title: CSRF on Password Reset Endpoint - No Anti-CSRF Token Required
description: The password reset endpoint at POST /password_reset on api.axross-recipe.com does not require any CSRF token, origin header check, or SameSite cookie validation. An attacker can craft a cross-origin HTML form that, when visited by a victim, silently triggers a password reset email to be sent to an arbitrary email address.
impact: An attacker can force a victim's browser to trigger password reset emails for arbitrary email addresses. This can be used for email bombing attacks, denial of service, or as a precursor to phishing attacks where the victim receives an unexpected password reset email from the legitimate service.
technical_analysis: The password reset endpoint at POST /password_reset on api.axross-recipe.com accepts JSON payloads with an email field. The endpoint returns {"result":"success"} for any email address. No CSRF token, Origin header, or Referer header validation is performed. The endpoint is accessible without authentication and without any session/cookie requirement. Additionally, there is no rate limiting on this endpoint, allowing an attacker to send unlimited password reset emails.
poc_description: 1. Send a POST request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/password_reset with JSON data containing an email field. 2. No CSRF token or session cookie is required. 3. The endpoint returns {"result":"success"} indicating the password reset email was sent. 4. This can be triggered cross-origin from an attacker-controlled website.
remediation_steps: 1. Implement CSRF protection on the password reset endpoint. 2. Validate the Origin and/or Referer headers. 3. Implement rate limiting on password reset requests per email address and per IP. 4. Add CAPTCHA or similar challenge to prevent automated abuse. 5. Consider implementing a time-based one-time password (TOTP) or email verification step before sending the reset email.

title: Open Redirect via NextAuth callbackUrl Parameter
description: The NextAuth signin endpoint at /api/auth/signin accepts an arbitrary callbackUrl parameter without validating that the URL is on the same origin. The callback URL is stored in the __Secure-next-auth.callback-url cookie and used to redirect the user after successful authentication. An attacker can craft a link that, when clicked, sets the callback URL to an external domain, leading to an open redirect after authentication.
impact: An attacker can use this open redirect for phishing attacks. After a victim authenticates via Azure AD, they would be redirected to an attacker-controlled domain. This can be used to steal authentication tokens, credentials, or trick users into visiting malicious sites. The open redirect can also be chained with OAuth flows to intercept authorization codes.
technical_analysis: The NextAuth.js signin endpoint at /api/auth/signin accepts a callbackUrl query parameter. When an external URL is provided (e.g., https://evil.com), the server sets the __Secure-next-auth.callback-url cookie to the external URL and redirects the browser to /signin?callbackUrl=https://evil.com. After the user completes authentication via Azure AD, the callback URL from the cookie is used to redirect the user. NextAuth.js by default validates callback URLs against the configured allowed origins, but the server accepts external URLs without validation. The cookie is set with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Lax attributes, but the URL itself is not validated against an allowlist.
poc_description: 1. Craft a URL: https://axross-recipe.com/api/auth/signin?callbackUrl=https://evil.com 2. When a victim visits this URL, the __Secure-next-auth.callback-url cookie is set to https://evil.com 3. The victim is redirected to /signin?callbackUrl=https://evil.com 4. If the victim authenticates via Azure AD, they would be redirected to https://evil.com after authentication
poc_script_code:
import requests
# Test the open redirect
url = "https://axross-recipe.com/api/auth/signin?callbackUrl=https://evil.com"
resp = requests.get(url, allow_redirects=False)
print(f"Status: {resp.status_code}")
print(f"Location: {resp.headers.get('Location')}")
for cookie in resp.cookies:
    print(f"Cookie: {cookie.name}={cookie.value}")
remediation_steps: 1. Validate the callbackUrl parameter against an allowlist of allowed origins. 2. Only allow relative paths or URLs on the same origin. 3. Implement a strict allowlist of callback URLs in the NextAuth configuration. 4. Consider using the NEXTAUTH_URL environment variable as the only allowed callback URL origin. 5. Add server-side validation that rejects callback URLs pointing to external domains.

title: Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication and Password Reset Endpoints
description: The signup endpoint (POST /signup) and password reset endpoint (POST /password_reset) on api.axross-recipe.com have no rate limiting. An attacker can send unlimited concurrent requests to these endpoints without any throttling or IP-based restrictions.
impact: An attacker can: 1. Create unlimited user accounts (account creation spam). 2. Send unlimited password reset emails to a target email address (email bombing). 3. Perform brute-force attacks on the login endpoint without rate limiting. 4. Exhaust server resources through rapid requests (denial of service).
technical_analysis: Testing confirmed that 10 concurrent requests to the signup endpoint all returned {"result":"success"} without any throttling. Similarly, 5 rapid requests to the password reset endpoint all returned success. No rate limiting headers (X-RateLimit-*) were observed in the responses. The server does not implement IP-based rate limiting, token bucket algorithms, or any other throttling mechanism on these endpoints.
poc_description: 1. Send 10 concurrent POST requests to https://api.axross-recipe.com/signup 2. All 10 requests return {"result":"success"} 3. Send 5 rapid POST requests to https://api.axross-recipe.com/password_reset 4. All 5 requests return {"result":"success"} 5. No rate limiting is observed
poc_script_code:
import concurrent.futures
import requests

def test_signup(i):
    url = "https://api.axross-recipe.com/signup"
    data = {"name": f"ratetest{i}", "email": f"ratetest{i}@test.com", "password": "TestPass123!"}
    resp = requests.post(url, json=data)
    return f"Request {i}: Status={resp.status_code}"

with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=10) as executor:
    futures = [executor.submit(test_signup, i) for i in range(10)]
    for future in concurrent.futures.as_completed(futures):
        print(future.result())
remediation_steps: 1. Implement rate limiting on all authentication and password reset endpoints. 2. Use IP-based rate limiting (e.g., 5 requests per minute per IP). 3. Implement account-based rate limiting (e.g., 3 password reset requests per hour per email). 4. Add CAPTCHA or similar challenge for signup and password reset flows. 5. Consider using a token bucket or sliding window algorithm for rate limiting. 6. Return appropriate HTTP status codes (429 Too Many Requests) with Retry-After headers when rate limits are exceeded.

title: CSRF on Login Endpoint - No Anti-CSRF Token Required
description: The login endpoint at POST /sessions on api.axross-recipe.com does not require any CSRF token, origin header check, or SameSite cookie validation. An attacker can craft a cross-origin HTML form that, when visited by a victim, silently attempts to log in with attacker-controlled credentials.
impact: An attacker can force a victim's browser to attempt authentication with attacker-controlled credentials. While the login itself would fail (wrong credentials), the request reveals the victim's IP address and user-agent to the attacker. More importantly, this CSRF vulnerability on the login endpoint demonstrates a systemic lack of CSRF protection across the API, increasing the risk for other state-changing operations.
technical_analysis: The login endpoint at POST /sessions on api.axross-recipe.com accepts JSON payloads with email_or_id and password fields. The endpoint returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid credentials, but does not require any CSRF token, Origin header, or Referer header validation. The endpoint is accessible without authentication. The API client (axios) sends requests with withCredentials: true, but the server does not validate the origin of the request.
poc_description: 1. Send a POST request to https://api.axross-recipe.com/sessions with JSON data containing email_or_id and password fields. 2. No CSRF token or session cookie is required. 3. The endpoint returns 401 Unauthorized for invalid credentials, but the request is processed without CSRF validation.
remediation_steps: 1. Implement CSRF protection on all state-changing API endpoints including login. 2. Validate the Origin and/or Referer headers on all state-changing requests. 3. Implement anti-CSRF tokens tied to the user session. 4. Use SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax cookies for session cookies.
